questions.stem: A 6 week old boy is brought to his GP because he is fussy during feeds. There are white patches on his tongue and inside his cheeks. When gently scraped with a spatula they come away, leaving a red, raw surface. He is gaining weight normally. His temperature is 36.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: White plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that scrape off to leave a red surface in an infant are oral candidiasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Scrapable white plaques with a red base in an infant.

elim: Aphthous ulcers are painful round ulcers, not white plaques.
This causes vesicles on hands, feet and mouth with fever.
Milk residue wipes off easily without leaving a red base.
Leukoplakia does not scrape off and is not seen in infants.

steps.x: **D. Oral candidiasis.** Oral thrush: infants, immunocompromised, inhaled steroid users.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman is having chemotherapy for breast cancer. She has a 5 day history of a sore mouth and altered taste. There are creamy white plaques on her tongue and soft palate that can be scraped off to reveal a red base. Her temperature is 37.0°C and neutrophil count 1.1 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Immunosuppression from chemotherapy allows Candida to overgrow, giving white plaques that scrape off to a red base.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: can be scraped off to reveal a red base
steps.x: Immunocompromised with scrapable white plaques.

elim: HSV causes painful vesicles and ulcers, not scrapable plaques.
Oral lichen planus is lacy and white and does not scrape off.
Mucositis causes red ulceration, not white scrapable plaques.
Hairy leukoplakia is on the side of the tongue and does not scrape off.

steps.x: **D. Oral candidiasis.** Candida overgrows with immune suppression or antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 5 day history of intense vulval itching and soreness. She has a thick, white, clumpy discharge with no smell. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has not had antibiotics recently. Her temperature is 36.8°C. The vulva is red and slightly swollen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Vulval itch with a thick, white 'cottage cheese' discharge and no odour is vaginal candidiasis; the combined pill is a risk factor.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: thick, white, clumpy discharge with no smell
steps.x: Itch, cottage cheese discharge, no odour.

elim: BV has a thin grey discharge with a fishy smell and little itch.
Chlamydia is often asymptomatic or causes bleeding, not itch.
Lichen sclerosus causes white atrophic skin, not discharge.
Trichomonas causes a frothy, yellow-green offensive discharge.

steps.x: **E. Vulvovaginal candidiasis.** Vaginal thrush: itch, cottage cheese discharge, no smell; OCP is a risk.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with obesity has a 3 week history of an itchy, sore rash in both groins. He works in a hot kitchen and sweats a lot. The rash is bright red and moist in the skin folds, with small separate red papules and pustules beyond its edge. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A red, moist rash in warm skin folds with satellite lesions is cutaneous candidiasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: small separate red papules and pustules beyond its edge
steps.x: Warm moist fold with satellite lesions.

elim: Erythrasma is brown and dry with no satellite lesions.
Flexural psoriasis is well-demarcated without satellite lesions.
Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects the scalp and face.
Tinea has an advancing scaly edge with central clearing and no satellite pustules.

steps.x: **A. Cutaneous candidiasis.** Cutaneous candidiasis: skin folds, red rash with satellite lesions.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with HIV who has not taken antiretrovirals for 2 years has a 4 week history of pain on swallowing and food sticking behind his sternum. He has lost 5 kg. His CD4 count is 60 cells/mm³ (500–1500). He has an upper GI endoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on endoscopy?
o: White plaques adherent to the oesophageal mucosa
questions.e: Dysphagia and odynophagia in advanced HIV is oesophageal candidiasis, an AIDS-defining illness, with white plaques on the mucosa.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Advanced HIV with dysphagia and odynophagia.

elim: Barrett's is from chronic reflux, not HIV.
That suggests CMV oesophagitis.
That suggests HSV oesophagitis.
Webs cause painless dysphagia.

steps.x: **E. White plaques adherent to the oesophageal mucosa.** Oesophageal candidiasis: AIDS-defining; dysphagia and odynophagia.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV. Her CD4 count is 80 cells/mm³ (500–1500). The HIV team reviews her history to decide whether she has AIDS. In the last 6 months she has had several of the conditions below.
questions.q: Which of these is an AIDS-defining illness?
questions.e: Oesophageal candidiasis is AIDS-defining because it reflects significant cell-mediated immunodeficiency; oral thrush alone is not.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Which Candida infection marks advanced immunodeficiency?

elim: Shingles is not AIDS-defining.
Oral thrush is common in HIV but is not AIDS-defining.
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is common but not AIDS-defining.
Vaginal thrush is not AIDS-defining.

steps.x: **B. Oesophageal candidiasis.** Oesophageal (not oral) candidiasis is AIDS-defining.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with acute myeloid leukaemia is neutropenic after chemotherapy. He has a central venous catheter and has had 10 days of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. He still has a fever of 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. Blood cultures grow yeast.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: In immunocompromised patients Candida can cause systemic (invasive) candidiasis; a central line and broad-spectrum antibiotics add risk.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Neutropenia, line, antibiotics, yeast in blood.

elim: There is no skin rash; the yeast is in the blood.
Blood cultures grew yeast, not bacteria.
Oral thrush does not cause yeast in the blood.
Pneumocystis does not grow in blood culture.

steps.x: **E. Systemic candidiasis.** Systemic candidiasis is the serious complication in the immunocompromised.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and obesity has a 2 week history of a sore, red, moist rash under both breasts. There are small red satellite papules beyond the edge. Skin scrapings show budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Budding yeast with satellite lesions in a warm skin fold is Candida, most commonly Candida albicans.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Skin fold, satellite lesions, budding yeast.

elim: That causes erythrasma, a dry brown rash.
Malassezia causes pityriasis versicolor on the trunk.
S. aureus is a bacterium and does not bud.
Dermatophytes form hyphae, not budding yeast, and cause ringed tinea.

steps.x: **A. Candida albicans.** Most common species: Candida albicans.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with asthma started a beclometasone inhaler 2 months ago. She uses it without a spacer. She now has a 1 week history of a sore mouth. There are white plaques on her tongue and palate that scrape off to leave a red base. She has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor?
o: Use of an inhaled corticosteroid without a spacer
questions.e: Inhaled corticosteroids cause local oropharyngeal immunosuppression, predisposing to oral candidiasis, especially without a spacer.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: scrape off to leave a red base
steps.x: New inhaled steroid, no spacer, oral thrush.

elim: The pill predisposes to vaginal, not oral, thrush.
There is nothing to suggest iron deficiency.
Not the classic predisposing factor here.
She has an obvious local cause.

steps.x: **E. Use of an inhaled corticosteroid without a spacer.** Inhaled steroids: oral thrush. Use a spacer and rinse the mouth.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man is on day 6 of IV co-amoxiclav for a chest infection. He now has a sore mouth and difficulty eating. There are white plaques on his tongue that scrape off to a red base. He has no history of diabetes, steroid use or immunosuppression. His temperature is 37.2°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his mouth problem?
questions.e: Antibiotics kill the competing normal flora, allowing Candida to overgrow and cause oral candidiasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: no history of diabetes, steroid use or immunosuppression
steps.x: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, no other risk factor.

elim: Allergy causes rash or urticaria, not scrapable plaques.
HSV causes vesicles and ulcers.
Glossitis is a smooth red tongue without plaques.
B12 deficiency causes glossitis, not white plaques.

steps.x: **B. Candida overgrowth after antibiotics.** Antibiotics or immunosuppression allow Candida overgrowth.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has a 4 day history of vulval itch and soreness after a course of clarithromycin. On examination there is vulval redness. Her temperature is 36.7°C. She is not pregnant and has no new sexual partner. The GP suspects vulvovaginal candidiasis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the discharge?
questions.e: Vaginal candidiasis gives a thick, white 'cottage cheese' discharge with no foul smell.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Itch after antibiotics.

elim: That is Trichomonas.
That suggests chlamydia or gonorrhoea.
That is bacterial vaginosis.
That raises concern about malignancy.

steps.x: **C. Thick, white, odourless discharge.** Thrush: cottage cheese, no smell. BV: fishy. Trich: frothy green.

questions.stem: A 9 month old girl has a 1 week history of a red nappy rash that has not improved with a barrier cream. The rash is bright red and involves the skin creases of the groin, with scattered red spots at its edges. She is otherwise well. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A red nappy rash involving the skin creases with satellite lesions, not responding to barrier cream, is cutaneous candidiasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: scattered red spots at its edges
not improved with a barrier cream
steps.x: Creases involved, satellite lesions.

elim: Atopic eczema usually spares the nappy area.
Irritant dermatitis spares the skin creases and has no satellite lesions.
Napkin psoriasis is well-demarcated without satellite spots.
Seborrhoeic dermatitis has greasy yellow scale.

steps.x: **B. Candidal nappy rash.** Candida involves skin folds with satellite lesions; irritant rash spares creases.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a vaginal discharge. The history is unclear: she reports mild itch but also some odour, and examination shows a white discharge. Her GP takes a vaginal swab for microscopy to confirm the cause. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which finding on microscopy would confirm candidiasis?
questions.e: Candidiasis is usually a clinical diagnosis; if confirmation is needed, microscopy shows budding yeast cells.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Atypical picture, so a swab is justified.

elim: Clue cells indicate bacterial vaginosis.
These indicate gonorrhoea.
These are Trichomonas.
Crystals indicate gout in joint fluid.

steps.x: **A. Budding yeast cells.** Microscopy: budding yeast (with pseudohyphae).

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has a first episode of vulval itch with a thick, white, odourless discharge after a course of amoxicillin. She has no other symptoms, is not pregnant and has no risk factors for sexually transmitted infection. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Candidiasis is usually diagnosed clinically from its characteristic appearance; a classic first episode needs no test.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Classic first episode with an obvious trigger.

elim: HbA1c is for recurrent candidiasis.
A swab is only needed if the symptoms are not typical.
Imaging has no role.
Not needed for a classic first episode.

steps.x: **C. No investigation: clinical diagnosis.** Usually a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with obesity has had four episodes of vulval itch with thick, white, odourless discharge in the past 10 months. Each settled with a single dose of fluconazole. She is not on any regular medication. Her temperature is 36.8°C and BMI is 36.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: High vaginal swab before any blood test
questions.e: Recurrent vaginal candidiasis needs an HbA1c to exclude diabetes; a vaginal swab is only needed if symptoms are not highly suggestive.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Recurrent classic thrush in an obese woman.

elim: Not relevant to recurrent thrush.
Not indicated.
A swab is only needed if the symptoms are not highly suggestive.
Imaging has no role.

steps.x: **C. HbA1c.** Recurrent vaginal thrush: HbA1c to exclude diabetes.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has had five episodes of vaginal discharge in a year. The discharge has sometimes been thin with a mild odour, and itching has been variable. Fluconazole helped only partly. Her HbA1c is 34 mmol/mol (20–41). Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Vaginal swab for microscopy and culture
questions.e: With diabetes excluded and symptoms not highly suggestive of thrush, a vaginal swab is taken to confirm the cause.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.

clues: sometimes been thin with a mild odour
steps.x: Atypical recurrent symptoms, diabetes excluded.

elim: Lipids do not explain recurrent discharge.
HbA1c is already normal.
Not relevant.
Not the next step.

steps.x: **E. Vaginal swab for microscopy and culture.** Swab only if symptoms are not highly suggestive.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has a first episode of vulvovaginal candidiasis with itch and thick, white, odourless discharge. She is not pregnant or breastfeeding. She has no other medical problems and takes no regular medication. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.e: A single episode of vaginal candidiasis is treated with oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose (topical clotrimazole is the alternative).

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
First episode, not pregnant.

elim: Three doses are for recurrent infection.
Metronidazole treats BV and Trichomonas.
Nystatin is for oral thrush.
Miconazole gel is for oral thrush.

steps.x: **A. Fluconazole 150 mg orally, single dose.** Single episode: fluconazole 150 mg PO once.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant has a 4 day history of vulval itch and a thick, white discharge with no odour. Her GP is about to prescribe oral fluconazole 150 mg. Her temperature is 36.8°C and BP 112/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: In pregnancy, oral fluconazole is avoided and an intravaginal clotrimazole pessary is used instead.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Pregnant with thrush.

elim: Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy.
Oral azoles are avoided in pregnancy.
Metronidazole is for BV and Trichomonas.
Symptomatic thrush should be treated.

steps.x: **A. Clotrimazole vaginal pessary.** Pregnancy: intravaginal clotrimazole.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a sore mouth with white plaques on his tongue that scrape off to a red base. He completed a course of amoxicillin last week. He takes no regular medication and has no drug allergies. His temperature is 36.9°C. The plaques are limited to the mouth.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Oral candidiasis is treated first-line with miconazole oral gel.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: scrape off to a red base
steps.x: Uncomplicated oral thrush, no interacting drugs.

elim: This does not treat Candida.
IV antifungals are for systemic candidiasis.
This treats HSV.
This is fungal, not bacterial.

steps.x: **C. Miconazole oral gel.** Oral thrush: miconazole oral gel.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with atrial fibrillation takes warfarin. He has oral candidiasis with white plaques on his tongue after a course of antibiotics. His INR has been stable. His temperature is 36.7°C. The pharmacist warns that miconazole oral gel interacts dangerously with warfarin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Miconazole oral gel with weekly INR
questions.e: Oral nystatin suspension is the alternative to miconazole gel, which raises the INR in patients on warfarin.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Oral thrush when miconazole cannot be used.

elim: This does not treat Candida.
The interaction is dangerous; use an alternative.
This treats HSV.
Stopping anticoagulation is unnecessary.

steps.x: **C. Nystatin oral suspension.** Oral alternative: nystatin suspension.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with COPD has extensive oral candidiasis with painful white plaques throughout her mouth and throat. A week of miconazole oral gel has not helped. She has no swallowing difficulty. Her temperature is 37.1°C. She takes no warfarin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Severe oral candidiasis not settling with topical treatment is treated with oral fluconazole.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Severe, failed topical therapy.

elim: This is for systemic candidiasis.
Cream is for skin.
Metronidazole is antibacterial.
Steroids worsen candidiasis.

steps.x: **C. Oral fluconazole.** Severe oral thrush: oral fluconazole.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman is not pregnant and has had six episodes of vulvovaginal candidiasis in the past year, each with typical itch and discharge. Her HbA1c is normal. Each episode has resolved with a single dose of fluconazole but keeps returning. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for this episode?
questions.e: Recurrent vaginal candidiasis is treated with an induction course of three doses of oral fluconazole 150 mg.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Recurrent, diabetes excluded.

elim: A single topical dose is undertreatment.
That is for a single episode.
Metronidazole does not treat Candida.
Douching worsens vaginal flora.

steps.x: **C. Fluconazole 150 mg orally, three doses.** Recurrent vaginal: fluconazole 150 mg x3.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man who is bedbound after a stroke has a red, moist rash in both groins and the gluteal fold with satellite papules. Skin scrapings show budding yeast. He is otherwise stable. His temperature is 36.8°C. There is no broken skin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Cutaneous candidiasis is treated with a topical antifungal such as clotrimazole or miconazole, with keeping folds dry.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: red, moist rash in both groins
steps.x: Skin fold Candida infection.

elim: Prolonged systemic therapy is unnecessary.
A potent steroid alone worsens fungal infection.
Fusidic acid is antibacterial.
Mupirocin is antibacterial.

steps.x: **C. Topical clotrimazole.** Cutaneous: topical clotrimazole or miconazole.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with asthma has had three episodes of oral thrush in a year. He uses a high-dose fluticasone inhaler. His asthma is well controlled and he does not want to stop it. Each episode settled with miconazole gel. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice to reduce recurrence?
o: Rinse his mouth and use a spacer with the inhaler
questions.e: Using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after an inhaled corticosteroid reduces local oropharyngeal steroid deposition and recurrence of oral candidiasis.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: does not want to stop it
steps.x: Recurrent ICS-related thrush.

elim: Prophylaxis is not first-line.
His asthma needs it.
Systemic steroids are worse overall.
Antibiotics increase Candida risk.

steps.x: **A. Rinse his mouth and use a spacer with the inhaler.** Prevention: spacer and rinse mouth.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman has taken oral doxycycline for acne for 3 months. She now has her third episode of vaginal thrush. She is otherwise healthy, with a normal HbA1c and no immunosuppression. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her recurrent infection?
o: Direct antibiotic toxicity to the vaginal wall
questions.e: Candida is normally kept in check by competing flora; antibiotics kill these bacteria and allow Candida to overgrow.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Long-term antibiotics, no other risk.

elim: Not the mechanism.
Her HbA1c is normal.
Thrush is not classically sexually transmitted.
She has no immunosuppression.

steps.x: **A. Antibiotics killing competing vaginal flora.** Disruption of flora (antibiotics) or immunity allows overgrowth.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with obesity has recurrent candidal infection under her breasts and in her groins every summer. Her HbA1c is normal. She works in a warm laundry. Her GP explains why Candida favours these particular sites. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Warm, moist environment in skin folds
questions.e: Warm, moist environments such as skin folds and mucosa favour Candida proliferation.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: under her breasts and in her groins
steps.x: Skin folds, worse in summer heat.

elim: Sebum favours Malassezia, not Candida.
Folds are shielded from light.
Not the key factor.
Not the mechanism.

steps.x: **E. Warm, moist environment in skin folds.** Candida likes warm, moist sites.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with asthma asks why her nurse advised her to rinse her mouth after each dose of her budesonide inhaler. She had oral thrush last year. She uses a spacer. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for this advice?
o: It improves absorption of the steroid
It prevents dental caries from the propellant
It reduces systemic steroid absorption causing diabetes
It removes steroid that causes local oropharyngeal immunosuppression
questions.e: Inhaled corticosteroids cause local immunosuppression in the oropharynx; rinsing and a spacer reduce deposition and oral thrush.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Advice after an inhaled steroid.

elim: Rinsing removes, not increases, steroid.
Not the reason.
Not the reason.
The main aim is to prevent oral thrush.

steps.x: **E. It removes steroid that causes local oropharyngeal immunosuppression.** ICS: local immunosuppression; rinse and spacer.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with untreated HIV has oesophageal candidiasis confirmed at endoscopy. His CD4 count is 45 cells/mm³ (500–1500). A student asks why this infection counts as AIDS-defining when vaginal thrush in healthy women does not.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Candida in the oesophagus is a different species
It is caused by antiretroviral drugs
questions.e: Oesophageal candidiasis is AIDS-defining because invasion beyond the mouth reflects significant cell-mediated (CD4 T-cell) immunodeficiency.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Deep mucosal Candida with very low CD4.

elim: It is still usually C. albicans.
He is untreated.
Candida is not an STI.
Cell-mediated, not antibody, immunity controls Candida.

steps.x: **B. It indicates significant cell-mediated immunodeficiency.** Oesophageal candidiasis = significant cell-mediated immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has itch and a thick white discharge and is treated with oral fluconazole for vaginal candidiasis. Her symptoms settle within 3 days. A pharmacology student asks which molecule in the fungal cell membrane is depleted by this drug, leading to membrane disruption.
questions.q: Which molecule is depleted?
questions.e: Azoles inhibit fungal cytochrome P450-dependent lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis and disrupting the fungal membrane.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Azole; fungal membrane sterol.

elim: Chitin is in the cell wall and targeted by other agents.
Cholesterol is the human membrane sterol.
Peptidoglycan is a bacterial wall component.
Echinocandins target β-glucan synthesis.

steps.x: **C. Ergosterol.** Azoles block lanosterol 14α-demethylase: no ergosterol.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has had three episodes of vulval itch with thick, white, odourless discharge in 6 months. She has also had thirst, nocturia and tiredness. She has had no recent antibiotics. Her temperature is 36.8°C and BMI 33. A random capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her recurrent infection?
questions.e: Recurrent vaginal candidiasis with osmotic symptoms and a high glucose points to diabetes, which is why HbA1c is checked in recurrent thrush.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Recurrent thrush with osmotic symptoms.

elim: She does not take it.
That predisposes to oral thrush.
She has had none.
Thrush is not sexually transmitted.

steps.x: **B. Diabetes mellitus.** Recurrent vaginal thrush: exclude diabetes with HbA1c.
